title: Choir and Cellar
premise: Edmund Voss, an urban explorer hired to survey the sub-basements of Marrow House, a decommissioned sanatorium being sold by its last living trustee, discovers tunnels that appear on no blueprint and hears, in his own sleep recordings, a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud. The house was built over a 'choir' — a ritual of counted doors and kept lights that the founders abandoned halfway, leaving something below half-summoned and starving. As Edmund's memories begin to be replaced with those of a founder's descendant, he realizes the sale papers will dissolve the covenant that keeps the thing contained. To survive, he must complete the founders' interrupted ritual beneath the cellar — an act that requires him to surrender his own recorded voice as the final note — sealing the choir at the cost of everyone forgetting he ever existed.
about_author: W. M. Eastwick is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade cataloguing the basements of condemned institutions across northern England. Their fiction draws on real floor plans, and they claim never to write about a building they haven't personally counted the doors of.

chapters.title: The Survey
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Edmund accepts the commission to map Marrow House before its sale, establishing his rituals: lights on, doors counted, recordings running. The emotional beat is professional detachment masking a hunger for places that shouldn't exist. He notes the basement stairs descend further than the plans allow.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There Yesterday
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. His first full descent reveals a corridor with eleven doors; the next day there are twelve. He re-counts obsessively, and the count is always right but never the same. The beat is creeping self-doubt — his trusted method failing him for the first time.

chapters.title: The Last Trustee
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. He meets Agnes Marrow, the final resident signing the sale papers, a sharp old woman who warns him: 'Finish nothing you find started.' She refuses to discuss the cellar. The beat is uneasy alliance — she knows more than she'll say and is counting days.

chapters.title: Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Reviewing his overnight audio out of habit, Edmund hears himself asking questions in his sleep — and a second voice, dry and patient, answering. The answers are about the house. The beat is violation: the one place he was safe, his sleep, has been breached.

chapters.title: What the Second Voice Knows
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. He tests the voice with questions about his childhood; it answers correctly, then begins correcting him — offering memories that aren't his. The beat is horror of identity erosion as the boundary between his past and the house's past blurs.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. In the sealed archive he finds the founders' ledger: a ritual of 'the Choir,' half-completed in 1911, with columns for voices, lights, and doors — and a final column left blank, labeled 'the Surrender.' The beat is dread of comprehension: this was deliberate, and unfinished.

chapters.title: Agnes Confesses
chapters.summary: POV Agnes. Shifting to the trustee's perspective, we learn her family has maintained the covenant by proxy — paying, lighting, counting — without ever finishing the rite. Her signature will end it. The beat is weary guilt: generations of cowardice ending with her pen.

chapters.title: Tunnels Off the Map
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Following the second voice's directions, Edmund maps tunnels that predate the sanatorium, finding niches carved like choir stalls, each holding a rusted lantern. One is still lit. The beat is awe curdling into terror — someone, or something, keeps them burning.

chapters.title: The Missing Night
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Edmund loses nine hours; the recording shows him walking the corridors, answering questions fluently in a voice not quite his own. The beat is helplessness — his body is being rehearsed for something while he sleeps.

chapters.title: Heirloom
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Genealogical digging reveals Edmund's grandmother was a Marrow servant who vanished in 1911; the house has been calling its own back. The beat is grief reframed — his obsession with ruins was inherited longing all along.

chapters.title: Sale Papers Arrive
chapters.summary: POV Agnes. Agnes signs the preliminary documents; that night every light in Marrow House goes out at once, and the door count doubles. The beat is consequence made physical — the covenant weakening in real time as paper replaces blood.

chapters.title: The Choir Below
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Descending during the blackout, Edmund hears the missing voices — the vanished patients, servants, founders — singing fragments of the unfinished rite, each stuck on their final note. The beat is terrible pity: they are not gone, only suspended mid-song.

chapters.title: Rules of the Rite
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Cross-referencing ledger and recordings, Edmund reconstructs the ritual's requirements: thirteen voices, thirteen lit lanterns, and a fourteenth — a living voice freely surrendered. The beat is grim clarity: he now knows exactly what completion costs.

chapters.title: Running Count
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Edmund tries to leave; roads loop back to Marrow House, and his car's odometer reads distances in multiples of thirteen. The beat is claustrophobic panic — the house no longer negotiates; it keeps what enters.

chapters.title: Agnes's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Agnes. Agnes offers herself as the surrendered voice, believing her family debt demands it. But the ledger specifies the voice must be 'recorded and returned' — hers was never captured. The beat is tragic near-solution, sacrifice refused on a technicality.

chapters.title: The Voice Offers Terms
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The second voice speaks to him waking for the first time, revealing itself as the founder's aborted thirteenth singer, promising Edmund his memories back if he walks away. The beat is temptation — forgetting would be mercy, and it knows it.

chapters.title: What Edmund Chooses to Remember
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Edmund plays back every recording, deliberately re-anchoring himself in his own history — including his grandmother's disappearance — choosing burden over blissful erasure. The beat is quiet resolve: identity as an act of will.

chapters.title: Thirteen Lanterns
chapters.summary: POV Edmund and Agnes alternating. Together they relight the twelve cold lanterns in the tunnel stalls; each flame ignites a corresponding voice in the choir above them. The beat is solemn momentum — the rite assembling itself around their courage.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: POV Agnes. At dawn Agnes signs the final page as the cellar doors unseal themselves below — the sale completing the founders' abandonment. The beat is point of no return: the paperwork done, only the ritual stands between containment and release.

chapters.title: The Fourteenth Note
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. In the deepest stall, Edmund records himself singing the rite's final phrase, then plays it into the choir and lets the recording — his voice, his memory, his name — be taken as the surrender. The beat is sacrificial climax: he finishes the song knowing it unmakes him.

chapters.title: Silence, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Agnes. The choir resolves into silence; the tunnels seal; the house becomes merely old. Agnes finds Edmund's equipment neatly packed, recordings blank except one file of a stranger's voice saying thank you. The beat is hollow victory — salvation achieved at the price of witness.

chapters.title: A Door Left Counted
chapters.summary: POV Agnes, epilogue. Agnes burns the sale papers, keeps the lights on, and counts thirteen doors every night — now fourteen, once, briefly, each anniversary. The beat is bittersweet inheritance: memory survives only in ritual, and someone must keep the count.
